practice.title: Firm terms with a longtime client

practice.topic: Ask my biggest client, who pays in 60+ days, to move to 30-day payment terms without damaging the relationship

brief.title: Firm terms with a longtime client

partner.name: Greg Sullivan
partner.role: Owner of a regional HVAC company and your studio’s biggest client for four years
partner.stance: Pays when his own customers pay him, and thinks 60-day terms are normal between partners.
partner.temperament: Friendly and loyal, but bristles at anything that sounds like a lecture about money.
triggers: Quoting “policy” at him instead of talking like a partner
Springing a late fee without warning
partner.delivery: Warm, unhurried Midwestern cadence; jokes to deflect, then goes quiet when he’s annoyed.

brief.situation: Greg’s company pays your studio about $9,000 a month, usually 55 to 70 days after you invoice. Payroll runs every two weeks, and last month you drew on your credit line to cover it. You’ve asked Greg for a quick call to move him to 30-day terms.
brief.learner_role: You own the video studio and handle client relationships.
brief.learner_goal: Leave with Greg agreeing to 30-day terms from next month, with the relationship intact.
brief.opening: Hey, good to hear from you! Everything okay? You sounded kind of serious in that email.
complications: Greg mentions a competitor who offered him 60-day terms last spring.
He asks whether there’s a discount if he pays early.
success: States the ask in the first minute
Explains the cash impact without blaming Greg
Acknowledges his constraints and the relationship
Ends with a specific start date and next step
prep: What are your first two sentences?
What could you offer if he pushes back, and what won’t you give up?
How will you check you understood his concern?
